executive_summary.company_overview: Thermify is a UK-based climate deeptech SME at TRL 6-7 that installs distributed micro data centres (HeatHubs) in domestic homes, using waste heat from cloud computing to replace gas boilers for space heating and hot water at low or no additional energy cost. The business model is dual-sided: B2B cloud clients pay for compute, subsidising residential heating costs, while the technology eliminates both data centre cooling waste and fossil-fuel boiler emissions simultaneously.
executive_summary.strongest_themes: Waste heat recovery, domestic decarbonisation, gas boiler replacement, and fuel poverty relief are the strongest funding themes. Thermify sits at the intersection of three active UK and EU policy priorities — residential net zero, data centre sustainability, and energy poverty — giving it unusually broad thematic reach across Innovate UK, DESNZ, Ofgem, and EIC programmes.
executive_summary.strongest_geographies: The UK is by far the strongest funding geography, with multiple active government and Innovate UK programmes directly targeting domestic decarbonisation and social housing retrofit. The EU (via Horizon Europe and the EIC) offers transformational scale-up funding if UK-Horizon association is confirmed for relevant programmes.
executive_summary.key_constraints: Three key constraints: (1) Several of the highest-value programmes (Ofgem SIF, Warm Homes: Social Housing Fund, NIA) require a licensed network operator or registered social landlord as lead applicant, meaning Thermify can only participate as a named partner rather than receiving grants directly. (2) UK re-association to Horizon Europe must be confirmed before committing resource to EIC applications. (3) The technology is sometimes positioned as an 'edge computing' play rather than a 'heating technology' — assessors from heat/buildings programmes may need to be convinced of the system's reliability and safety as a primary heating source.

strategic_recommendations.best_fit_strategy: Pursue a two-track approach: (A) invest significant effort in the EIC Accelerator Deep Tech Climate Adaptation Challenge 2026 as the single highest-upside opportunity — it is a named, specific competition with near-perfect thematic alignment and transformational funding potential; (B) in parallel, maintain a steady cadence of UK direct-grant applications (EEF, Innovate UK Smart Grants, Net Zero Living) which are lower stakes but more predictable. Simultaneously build network operator and RSL partnerships to unlock the partner-route programmes (SIF, WHSHF, NIA) which represent the largest volume of available UK innovation funding.
strategic_recommendations.best_geographies: United Kingdom (primary — most accessible, most thematically aligned, lowest eligibility risk) and EU via Horizon/EIC (secondary — transformational scale, but contingent on UK association confirmation).
strategic_recommendations.strongest_pathways: Priority order: (1) EIC Accelerator Deep Tech Climate Challenge 2026 — single most important opportunity; begin preparing the short proposal immediately. (2) Energy Entrepreneurs Fund Phase 10 — monitor DESNZ closely for opening announcement; this is the most natural UK government fit. (3) Innovate UK Smart Grants / Net Zero Living — maintain rolling readiness to apply when a specific competition opens. (4) Ofgem SIF / NIA as partner — identify a DNO or GDN co-development partner to unlock these routes.
strategic_recommendations.key_partnerships: Three partnership types would materially unlock funding: (1) A licensed Distribution Network Operator (e.g. UK Power Networks, Northern Powergrid) or Gas Distribution Network (e.g. Cadent, SGN) as lead applicant for Ofgem SIF and NIA projects. (2) A registered social landlord or housing association with social housing stock to co-apply for Warm Homes: Social Housing Fund Wave 4. (3) A European university or research institute to enable EIC Transition consortium applications and Horizon CL5 participation.
strategic_recommendations.capability_gaps: Thermify should build and document: (1) rigorous carbon savings data per HeatHub installation (kgCO2e/year, compared to gas boiler baseline) — this is essential for all heat decarbonisation grant applications; (2) a credible cost-per-household model showing lifecycle economics versus heat pumps and gas boilers; (3) safety and reliability certification data, particularly for social housing contexts where landlord liability is a concern; (4) a clear grid interaction narrative explaining how HeatHub deployment affects local electricity demand, to appeal to Ofgem-funded programmes.
strategic_recommendations.key_risks: Main risks: (1) UK-Horizon association status — if UK SMEs cannot access EIC Accelerator 2026, the highest-priority opportunity falls away; verify this immediately. (2) Competition risk on EIC Accelerator — success rates are approximately 5-10% and require extensive proposal development investment. (3) Programme continuity risk on EEF — Phase 10 has not been confirmed; DESNZ budget pressures could delay or cancel it. (4) Assessor unfamiliarity — HeatHub straddles computing infrastructure and domestic heating, and may not be immediately legible to assessors from either sector; clear, jargon-free framing is essential.

company_profile.name: Thermify
company_profile.value_proposition: Thermify replaces domestic gas boilers by installing distributed micro data centres (HeatHubs) in homes, using the waste heat from cloud computing to heat homes and hot water at no additional energy cost.
company_profile.technology: Patented HeatHub units containing ~500 Raspberry Pi Compute Modules submerged in dielectric oil, installed in domestic properties; heat generated by cloud computing tasks is captured and transferred to the home's central heating system, effectively using each unit of electricity twice — once for compute and once for heat. Business clients pay Thermify for cloud processing, subsidising the householder's heating.
company_profile.primary_outcome: Reduction in household carbon emissions and energy bills by replacing gas boilers with waste-heat recovery from distributed edge computing nodes
secondary_benefits: Eliminates need for active cooling in traditional data centres, reducing overall data centre energy consumption
Provides affordable heat to low-income and social housing residents
Offers businesses an environmentally friendly cloud computing alternative
Generates contracted revenue from B2B cloud clients to fund household deployments
company_profile.trl: TRL 6-7 — live pilot installs in domestic homes (including social housing trials and a widely reported BBC case study), with £2.5m contracted revenue and patented technology, but not yet at full commercial scale
company_profile.website_summary: Thermify is a UK climate tech company that installs small distributed data centre units (HeatHubs) inside domestic homes, using the heat generated by cloud computing workloads to replace gas boilers for space heating and hot water. Business clients pay Thermify to process their cloud computing tasks via the HeatHub network, meaning the householder receives heat at low or no additional cost. The model uses each unit of electricity twice — for compute and for heat — eliminating the waste inherent in both conventional data centres and fossil-fuel boilers.
company_profile.external_findings: Thermify has live pilot installations in UK homes, including a high-profile BBC feature (November 2025) showcasing a family heating their Essex home via a shed-based HeatHub, and a social housing trial reported by Techerati. The company reports £2.5m in contracted B2B cloud revenue and holds a patent on its technology; it has also been validated through SPECIFIC IKC's performance data programme in Wales. Thermify is actively seeking equity investment via Republic Europe crowdfunding (as of April 2026), having already secured £1m in off-platform investment as part of a broader funding round.
